analysis.one_liner: Bars most lawsuits against makers of workplace equipment once the product is 12 years old.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved it 21-12, but the bill never received a floor vote before Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set a 12-year federal cutoff, called a statute of repose, on lawsuits against manufacturers and sellers of durable goods used in businesses — things like industrial machinery, farm equipment, and construction tools. After 12 years from the product's first sale, an injured worker could not sue the maker for death or injury, as long as the worker was covered by workers' compensation, and property damage claims would also be barred. It would override state laws that allow lawsuits over older products.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers and sellers of long-lasting workplace equipment gain the most: after 12 years, they would face no lawsuit risk for injuries or property damage their products cause, even for defects that existed when the product was built. Their liability insurers would also benefit from lower exposure.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Durable goods makers and their insurers

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars civil suits against a manufacturer or seller of a durable good for property damage occurring more than 12 years after the product was first sold or leased [S3][S4].

It also bars suits for death or personal injury more than 12 years after first sale, when the injured person received or was eligible for workers' compensation and the injury is not a toxic harm such as asbestos exposure [S3][S4].
The cutoff would preempt state statutes of repose, replacing state law with a uniform national 12-year limit [S4].
It preserves a few exceptions: products under longer written safety warranties, fraudulently hidden defects, environmental cleanup claims, and government regulatory actions [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Injured workers and their families would bear the cost. A person hurt by a defective 13-year-old machine — a lathe, a press, a tractor — would generally have no right to sue the maker, with the costs of the injury falling on workers' compensation systems and on the injured worker's own losses. Small businesses whose workers are not eligible for workers' compensation, and anyone suing over property damage from old equipment, would also lose their day in court.

drawbacks.text: The bill shifts injury costs from manufacturers to workers: a worker hurt by an aging but defective machine would be limited to workers' compensation, which typically pays far less than a jury award for a catastrophic injury [S3][S4].

The fraudulent-concealment exception is narrow — it requires proving the maker actually knew of the defect, that the defect caused the harm, and that the maker deliberately hid it to deceive — a high bar that few injured workers could meet [S4].
The bill applies retroactively: it would take effect immediately and could cut off claims that were still legally available when it passed, with only a one-year grace period for filing [S4].
It is a one-size-fits-all federal rule that overrides the statutes of repose states have chosen for themselves, including states with longer or no such limits [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Manufacturers argue a hard cutoff brings certainty and lowers liability costs that get built into equipment prices. The cost falls on a narrow group of injured workers and small businesses, who would lose the ability to hold a maker accountable for a defective old machine — and the one-year retroactive window could wipe out existing claims. On balance, this is a transfer of legal risk away from manufacturers and onto workers.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved it 21-12 in July 2006 and reported it on December 8, 2006, and it was placed on the House calendar, but the House never voted on it before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Chabot introduced the bill on July 28, 2005, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1][S6].

The Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law held a hearing in March 2006, and the full committee held markup sessions before ordering the bill reported on a 21-12 vote on July 19, 2006 [S6].
The committee reported an amended version on December 8, 2006, adding exceptions for regulatory enforcement actions and for manufacturers who fraudulently concealed a defect [S3][S6].
The House Energy and Commerce Committee was discharged from further consideration the same day, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills ready for a floor vote [S6].
The House adjourned for the end of the 109th Congress without ever taking a floor vote, so the bill died on January 3, 2007 [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured workers kept their existing right to sue over older defective equipment, because the bill never became law. Manufacturers of long-lasting workplace equipment did not get the 12-year shield they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured workers, who kept their right to sue

industries.industry: Manufacturers of durable workplace goods (industrial machinery, construction and farm equipment)
industries.note: The bill would have cut off lawsuits against them for injuries and property damage caused by products more than 12 years old, eliminating liability for defects that surface late in a machine's life. The gain comes directly at the expense of injured workers, whose recovery would be limited to workers' compensation.

industries.industry: Liability insurers for equipment makers and sellers
industries.note: A 12-year repose removes a large tail of old-product claims, reducing insurers' exposure. The savings come from claims that would otherwise compensate injured workers.
Most claims against makers of old workplace equipment would be barred, eliminating work in this area. Their loss mirrors the loss of legal recourse for injured workers.
